2. scout checks what actually changed
3. quant compares the last saved state
4. risk returns PASS / CUT / KILL
5. exec handles safe, approved actions
6. scribe logs every run and queues drafts

the trick isn't making 6 bots work harder. it's stopping them from waking up for nothing.

add a cheap change check before every full run and my cost model drops from $397 to $45 (-89%).

anything risky at 3 a.m. stays a draft until you're awake.

that's the Grok Bot setup i'd actually trust overnight.

hits.text:
i can’t believe people still send every task to Opus

one Jev call in front of your agent and every task finds its tier:

→ Jev reads the task and picks small, mid or frontier
→ Haiku and Sonnet take the easy work
→ Opus 5.5 only gets the hard stuff
→ a Jev guard checks every bash command before it runs

the router costs $0.042 per million tokens.

output is free.

paste this into claude code 👇

claude plugin marketplace add typesafe-ai/skills
claude plugin install typesafe@typesafe-ai
Add a Jev router and a Jev command guard to this project.
Router: before each task, ask Jev (jev-latest) one choice question (small, mid, frontier) and one noul question (plan before editing?). Map small to Haiku 5.5, mid to Sonnet 5.5, frontier to Opus 5.5. Low confidence routes up a tier, never down.
Guard: a PreToolUse hook on Bash that asks Jev if the command is destructive. Under 0.35 run it, 0.35 to 0.7 ask me, over 0.7 deny.
Read TYPESAFE_API_KEY from env, time out after 4 seconds, and fall back to asking me.
Show me the diff before changing anything.

All the facts in both posts come from published sources: the install commands, Jev’s pricing, the force push and rm example scores, and Opus at $4 / $20.

hits.text:
GPT 5.1 and Opus 5.5 both nail the first 3D model, but by the tenth edit one of them is rewriting parts nobody asked it to touch

A first draft is a demo. Revision is the real job, and it shows whether a model remembers what you already approved.

> DRAFT - one identical description, both models produce a full rigged object
> EDIT - ten small change requests in a row, each one touching a single part
> DIFF - after every round the whole file compared against the version before it
> DRIFT - any change outside the requested part counted as damage, however small

Round one was a draw. Both objects were clean, sensibly rigged and close to the brief.

GPT 5.1 started drifting by round three. Ask for a thicker handle and the lid’s proportions shifted along with it.

It was regenerating the whole object each time and calling it an edit. The parts you signed off on kept moving under you.

Opus 5.5 changed what was asked and left everything else identical, all the way through round ten.

That sounds minor until a client approves the base in round two and spots it changed in round nine.

Every silent change means a re-review. Ten edits with drift is ten full inspections instead of ten quick glances.

The test anyone can run is boring and brutal: request one tiny change, then diff everything that was not part of it.

Scroll to the next post for both edit logs and every diff, round one to round ten.

I COMBINED IT WITH MY GROK BOT CONTENT CREATION SETUP. NOW IT HELPS ME FIND IDEAS WORTH MAKING.

Grok Bot can search, read, and monitor X directly. You give it a task inside Grok Bot, and it gets to work.

It already had an X API integration. The latest update goes further: searching, reading, and monitoring no longer require setting up the X connector.

Here’s where this gets interesting for creators:

→ Find conversations gaining attention in your niche
→ Research new tools and product announcements
→ Pull out the questions people keep asking
→ Turn those findings into original content angles

A request you can try:

“Find posts in my niche gaining traction in the last 24 hours. Include source links, explain what people are responding to, and suggest five original video ideas for my audience.”

That research feeds into my existing Grok Bot content setup.

Now the setup has a way to discover what people are talking about before I decide what to make next.

For my X workflow, Grok Bot is my pick for the best agent right now.

Finding a good idea is often the part that stops you from making anything. Give the bot a clear niche, a time window, and an output you can actually use.

One useful research brief can give you somewhere to start today.

Anthropic put a model on the question of how viruses hijack the ribosome, and caught a few of them politely waiting in line instead of cutting it

A virus is supposed to seize the machinery. Shut the host down, take every ribosome, build nothing but itself.

> READ - the translation machinery of infected cells tracked instead of the virus alone
> SPLIT - host proteins separated from viral ones at every point in the infection
> RATE - how fast each side is being built measured hour by hour
> STOP - the moments the virus could have seized control and did not
> LAST - each strategy set against how long the infected cell survives

The aggressive ones are easy to spot. Host production collapses, viral protein floods out, and the cell dies fast.

A small group does the opposite. They take a modest share of the ribosomes and let the cell keep making its own proteins.

Those infections last far longer. A living cell is a working factory, and the virus keeps a factory rather than a corpse.

That restraint is also why they go unnoticed. Nothing crashes, so nothing alerts the host to a problem.

It reframes what a successful virus looks like. Not the fastest takeover, but the one that never triggers the alarm.

Antivirals are built to interrupt a seizure. There is nothing to interrupt when the virus is simply queuing.

The restrained strains and the share of ribosomes each one takes are broken down underneath.

Opus 5.5 rebuilt the Moon in Blender from public elevation data, and the lighting test exposed craters that never see a sunrise

The geometry was the easy half. What matters is that every height is a measurement, so the shadows fall where real ones do.

> MESH - public lunar elevation loaded as raw numbers and built to scale, nothing smoothed
> SPIN - the Sun driven across a full lunar cycle instead of posed for one render
> DARK - every point that never receives direct light ranked by how long it stays cold

A textured sphere looks right from any angle and tells you nothing. Only real elevation produces real shadow.

The polar craters are where it gets interesting. Their rims are tall enough that the floor stays dark through every cycle.

Those floors are among the coldest places in the solar system, and that is exactly why water ice can sit there.

The same pass finds the opposite too: ridges that catch sunlight almost permanently, which is where a base would want its panels.

None of this needs a lab. The elevation data is public, Blender is free, and the physics does the rest.

Most people treat 3D as decoration. Build it from measurements and it stops illustrating and starts answering.

The scene file, the data source and the full shadow map sit in the breakdown below.

-> before a plan: is this the right approach?
-> when the same error keeps coming back: am I digging in the wrong place?

press Ctrl+O to read what it told Opus

the clever part: toggling /advisor leaves the Opus prompt cache intact, so you only pay for the few moments Fable actually reads the session

and when the advice clashes with what's in the files, Opus flags the conflict and keeps going on the evidence

it's the core idea of Jev engineering: the expensive model stays out of routine steps and only shows up where the outcome can change

> Opus 5.5 on high runs the main session
> subagent one reads code
> subagent two edits and runs tests

outsiders.text:
Okay I've been going hog wild on Claude Code, ChatGPT Dot (desktop), and Grok Bot the last couple days and yeah my opinion of Grok Bot remains unchanged. 

It is the derpiest of the lot. 

For instance, I gave it a rule that agent-to-agent communication is always whitelisted (which uses the grok bot email as well as my personal email) and EVERY TIME it asks permission. I give it permission, update the rule, and ask it to verify the rule.

Then it asks again.

So like yeah the form factor of Grok Bot was good as a first mover but the underlying model remains dumb AF. So aggressively stupid. 

I only had to explain the rule to ChatGPT once. 

Grok Bot also still refuses to tell me what the backing model is, so that doesn't engender trust. 

Hopefully poteto will work on this (or someone) but yeah, my impression of Grok and Grok Bot remains unchanged. This is the most consistently disappointing AI out there. 

Now, I really wish Gemini had this capability because it genuinely thinks differently. It has a different set of failure modes, but it would add genuine entropy and eccentricity. 

So, we still have the duopoly of OpenAI and Anthropic as the only really useful frontier companies for this kind of agentic work. 

Yes, I know that plenty of open weight and other models are great if you want to get deep in harness-land but I don't. I just want something that works out of the box.
